questions.q: State the one-word property that makes the median a better choice than the mean when a data set contains extreme outliers.
questions.a: Resistant (or resistance). A wrong answer like "middle" or "position" shows the student knows how to find the median but does not understand the statistical property that justifies its use over the mean in the presence of outliers.

questions.q: A teacher calculates the mean and median of a class test. The mean is 72 and the median is 78. Without seeing the data, what can you infer about the shape of the distribution and why?
questions.a: The distribution is left-skewed (negatively skewed) with a tail toward lower scores. Because the mean is pulled toward the tail while the median stays closer to the bulk of the data, a mean lower than the median indicates low outliers or a long left tail. A student who says "right-skewed" confuses the direction of pull; a student who says "symmetric" does not grasp that mean and median differ exactly when the distribution is asymmetric.

questions.q: The monthly pocket money (in ₹) of 7 friends is: 200, 250, 250, 300, 300, 300, 2000. Calculate both measures and state which better represents the typical pocket money. Show your work.
questions.a: Mean = (200+250+250+300+300+300+2000)/7 = 3600/7 ≈ ₹514.29. Ordered data: 200, 250, 250, 300, 300, 300, 2000. Median = 4th value = ₹300. The median (₹300) is better because the ₹2000 is an outlier that inflates the mean far above what 6 out of 7 friends receive. A student who picks the mean likely computed correctly but missed the interpretation step; a student who miscalculates the median (e.g., averages the two middle values) forgets that n=7 is odd.

questions.q: Two data sets have the same median (50) but different means: Set A mean = 50, Set B mean = 65. Compare the likely shapes of the two distributions and explain what the difference in means tells you about the values in each set.
questions.a: Set A is roughly symmetric (mean ≈ median). Set B is right-skewed (mean > median), indicating a few unusually high values pulling the mean upward while the median remains at 50. The higher mean in Set B does NOT mean the "typical" value is higher; it means the distribution has a long right tail. A student who claims Set B has generally higher values confuses mean with typical value and does not understand that median represents the typical value in skewed data.

questions.q: A student argues: "The mean is always better because it uses all the data points, while the median ignores most of them." Evaluate this statement and give a counterexample where the mean gives a misleading picture.
questions.a: The statement is false. Using all data points is a weakness when some points are errors or extreme outliers. Counterexample: House prices in a locality (in lakhs): 40, 42, 45, 48, 50, 55, 500. Mean = 111.4, Median = 48. The mean suggests a typical price of ₹1.11 crore, but 6 out of 7 houses are around ₹40-55 lakhs. The median correctly represents the typical price. A student who agrees with the statement confuses "using more information" with "giving a better summary" and misses the concept of resistance.

questions.q: Create a real-life scenario (Indian context) with 8 data values where the median is at least 20% less than the mean. List the values, calculate both measures, and explain why the median is the appropriate summary.
questions.a: Example: Daily wages (₹) of 8 workers: 300, 300, 300, 350, 350, 400, 400, 5000. Mean = 7900/8 = ₹987.5. Median = (350+350)/2 = ₹350. Median is 64.6% less than mean. The ₹5000 is an outlier (maybe a supervisor). The median reflects the typical worker's wage. A poor answer would use a symmetric set (mean≈median) or fail to show the 20% gap, indicating the student cannot engineer skewness.
